issues.description: Fast-path predicate HAS_TIME is under-specified and not reasoned about
issues.detail: The regex /\dm?s/i is offered as a cheap pre-filter, but the author has stated no precondition for what constitutes a 'time value' nor proved that every input the downstream valueParser would have flagged is matched by this predicate. The pattern matches any digit followed by optional 'm' and then 's' anywhere in the string. Consider strings like 'gaps' (contains 'gs'? no, but '1gs' would match), 'red 0px solid' (no match, fine), 'translate3d(...)' — '3d' no; but 'mass 1s' matches and is fine, while constructed values like 'var(--x)' containing a digit-then-s in a fallback could match spuriously. More worryingly, a unit-less time would be missed — though CSS time tokens require a unit, so this is likely safe. The point is the author has not written down which set of strings is being filtered, and the reviewer is left to enumerate the cases.

issues.description: Regex is anchorless and case-insensitive, doing more work than necessary
issues.detail: /\dm?s/i with the /i flag is required only for the 'm' and 's' letters; since CSS units are case-insensitive this is correct, but a non-capturing, non-i form like /\d(?:ms|s)/i (or character class) would communicate intent more precisely. As written, the predicate also matches 'gs', 'es', '7s' inside identifiers or var() fallbacks, which the downstream parser must still reject. This is harmless for correctness but the choice was not justified in the changeset.

issues.description: No invariant or postcondition stated; correctness rests on testing
issues.detail: The patch reorders work: cheap predicate first, expensive parse second. The invariant the author needs is: HAS_TIME.test(v) === false implies valueParser(v) would yield timeValueCount === 0 for this rule. That implication is not proved, only assumed. The existing test suite presumably still passes, which under Dijkstra's discipline is evidence of the presence of correctness but not its absence — TESTED-NOT-PROVED. A one-line comment naming the invariant would convert this from folklore to reasoning.

'Fixed: time-min-milliseconds performance' tells the reader nothing about magnitude, mechanism, or risk. A patch-level changeset entry should at minimum name what was slow and what made it fast (early-exit on a regex pre-check) so a future maintainer reading the log can reason about the change without re-deriving it from the diff.

review.summary: The patch adds a cheap regex pre-filter before the expensive valueParser call — a sound optimization in spirit, and the structured control flow is unobjectionable (an early return is a permitted structured exit here, not a smuggled goto). What the patch lacks is reasoning written down: the author does not state the invariant that HAS_TIME.test(v) === false implies valueParser would have found no time values, and so the correctness of the optimization rests on the test suite rather than on proof. TESTED-NOT-PROVED. The regex /\\dm?s/i is slightly looser than the set of valid CSS time tokens and will admit false positives that the parser must still reject — harmless for correctness, but a more precise predicate (e.g. /\\d(?:ms|s)\\b/i or matching the actual time-value grammar) would make the invariant obvious by inspection. Verdict: accept with the requirement that the author add one comment naming the precondition the fast-path preserves, and tighten the regex or justify its looseness.
